description: English Foundation year width tiers — all 29 descriptors across Language, Literature and Literacy strands.
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term at Foundation level. For concept standards: the minimum phenomena or contexts that still genuinely meet the command term. For capability standards: the narrowest task context in which the skill is demonstrated. Foundation minimum is deliberately narrow — beginning literacy and language understanding is the starting point.
width_notes.typical_width: The full descriptor scope as ACARA intended at Foundation, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects what a well-taught Foundation class would have engaged with across the year.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or task types — not harder versions of the same activity. At Foundation, wider directions introduce additional text types, cultural contexts (especially First Nations), multimodal forms, or cross-curricular vocabulary connections.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data for typical_width and to identify wider directions. Not treated as a checklist — some elaborations are merged, some inform wider items. First Nations elaborations are always included in wider.

AC9EFLA01.minimum_width: Identify that language used at school differs from language used at home; give one example of each.
AC9EFLA01.typical_width: Recognise and explore how language changes depending on the relationship between people (parent/child, teacher/student, friends); practise asking questions, making requests and expressing opinions in school-appropriate ways.
wider: Explore language differences across a range of community settings; for example, how you speak to a shopkeeper, a family friend, or a community elder
Identify how language in picture books or simple stories reflects different relationship types and compare with classroom language
Discuss how words and tone in First Nations Australian storytelling contexts may differ from everyday classroom language
elaborations: asking relevant questions, and expressing requests and opinions in ways that suit the contexts
learning to use language according to the relationship between people; for example, between a parent and a child, a teacher and a student, siblings or friends, shopkeepers and customers

AC9EFLA02.minimum_width: Identify at least one word or phrase used to express a like or dislike.
AC9EFLA02.typical_width: Explore a range of ways to express preferences, likes and dislikes in speech and gesture; recognise how feelings and preferences can be communicated in visual texts such as advertising and animations.
wider: Compare how characters in different picture books express preferences and feelings — including books by First Nations Australian authors
Explore how simple digital or media texts (animations, advertisements) use visual cues alongside language to express feelings
Investigate how preference language changes across different community or cultural contexts familiar to students
elaborations: recognising how feelings and preferences might be communicated in speech and gesture
recognising the ways emotions and feelings can be conveyed in visual and media texts; for example, in advertising and animations

AC9EFLA03.minimum_width: Identify at least two different text forms (e.g. a sign and a book) and recognise they have different purposes.
AC9EFLA03.typical_width: Recognise that texts take many forms (signs, books, digital texts, labels, instructions); identify texts in school, home and community settings and explain what each is for; understand that First Nations Australians' stories may be oral or image-based.
wider: Compare how information is presented differently in a crossing sign versus a set of written instructions — examining layout, images and words
Explore First Nations Australian stories from oral, visual and digital sources and discuss how these differ from print books
Investigate multimodal texts such as websites or apps and identify text forms not typically found in print
elaborations: comparing images in informative and imaginative texts, and identifying similarities and differences
comparing different ways information might be presented; for example, on a sign or in a set of instructions
identifying different forms of texts in school, home and community settings; for example, crossing signs, hand washing signs, directions and product labels
understanding that many First Nations Australians' stories are oral narrations and cultural accounts, and may be represented as or with images

AC9EFLA04.minimum_width: Demonstrate that written text is read left-to-right and that books have a title and a starting place.
AC9EFLA04.typical_width: Understand and apply print conventions: left-to-right directionality, top-to-bottom, title identification, where to start reading; identify image and word placement on a page; identify basic navigation features of digital texts such as tabs.
wider: Compare print and screen text conventions — for example, how a digital text navigated by tabs differs from a book with a table of contents
Explore texts in languages written in different directions (right-to-left or vertically) and compare conventions with English
Investigate how layout choices (placement of images vs words) affect how a reader approaches a text
elaborations: learning that Standard Australian English in written texts is read from left to right and usually from top to bottom of the page
identifying tabs in a digital text
discussing the placement of images and words in text
indicating the title of a book and where to start reading

AC9EFLA05.minimum_width: Distinguish a sentence from a sentence fragment; recognise that sentences express a complete idea.
AC9EFLA05.typical_width: Recognise that sentences are key units of meaning; understand that word order matters for meaning; identify the difference between a sentence fragment and a complete sentence across multiple examples.
wider: Experiment with reordering words in simple sentences to see how meaning changes (e.g. 'The boy sat on the dog' vs 'The dog sat on the boy')
Identify sentences in a range of familiar texts — books, signs, labels — and discuss what makes them complete
Play with constructing and breaking sentences deliberately as a metalinguistic game
elaborations: learning that word order in sentences is important for meaning; for example, "The boy sat on the dog." "The dog sat on the boy."
recognising the difference between a sentence fragment and a sentence; for example, "after school", "Dad will pick me up after school."

AC9EFLA06.minimum_width: Identify that words in a sentence work together; give one example of a noun and a verb working together.
AC9EFLA06.typical_width: Recognise that sentences are made of groups of words that work together to make meaning; identify how a noun connects to a verb and how an adjective connects to a noun across simple examples.
wider: Sort words in simple sentences into functional groups (who/what, doing, describing) using physical sorting activities
Explore how changing one word in a sentence changes meaning — swapping nouns, verbs or adjectives
Identify word relationships in a range of text types: picture books, simple informative texts and labels
elaborations: learning how words in a sentence relate to one another; for example, connecting a cat (noun) to ate (verb), or black (adjective) to a cat (noun)

AC9EFLA07.minimum_width: Identify that images and words together make meaning in one text; note one thing conveyed by images but not words (or vice versa).
AC9EFLA07.typical_width: Explore the contribution of images and words to meaning in both stories and informative texts; recognise that texts can be interpreted differently when only words or only images are attended to; identify where images extend or contradict written text.
wider: Compare image-word relationships across a range of text types — picture books, informative texts, digital animations — noting different conventions
Create a simple multimodal text using drawing and labels, then discuss what each mode contributes
Explore texts by First Nations Australian illustrators and discuss how visual elements carry cultural meaning alongside or beyond the words
elaborations: recognising that texts can be interpreted differently when only the words or only the images are read or viewed
identifying where written text is reflected in accompanying images and where written text is not captured in images

AC9EFLA08.minimum_width: Recognise and use vocabulary relevant to at least one familiar context (e.g. topic studied at school).
AC9EFLA08.typical_width: Recognise and develop awareness of vocabulary across everyday experiences, personal interests and school topics; expand vocabulary through interactions, texts, images and objects; use topic-specific words in both imaginative and informative contexts.
wider: Connect topic vocabulary from one learning area to another — for example, 'habitat' in science and 'setting' in English
Investigate how vocabulary differs across community and cultural contexts familiar to students, including First Nations Australian language words where relevant
Develop vocabulary through play-based experiences, role-play and dramatisation across multiple topics
elaborations: identifying learning area–specific words when learning new topics or engaging in imaginative play; for example, role-playing a shopkeeper and a customer
identifying words for a topic studied at school; for example, words relevant to the topic of families
expanding vocabulary through informal interactions and planned experiences with adults and peers, texts, images, and artefacts or objects

AC9EFLA09.minimum_width: Identify punctuation marks as different from letters; recognise that capital letters signal names and sentence beginnings.
AC9EFLA09.typical_width: Identify punctuation as a distinct feature of written text; recognise capital letters for names and at sentence beginnings; recognise that punctuation marks signal sentence endings; notice these features across a range of everyday and classroom texts.
wider: Identify and sort different punctuation marks encountered across a variety of text types — books, labels, signs, digital texts
Compare how capital letters appear in own name, classmates' names, school name and text titles — exploring the consistency of the rule
Explore how punctuation marks are used in different ways in digital texts (e.g. emoji functioning as punctuation in informal messages)
elaborations: commenting on capital letters encountered in everyday texts; for example, "That's the letter that starts my name." "The name of my family and my town have capital letters."

AC9EFLE01.minimum_width: Share an idea about one story or image and connect it to a personal experience.
AC9EFLE01.typical_width: Share ideas about stories, poems and images; reflect on experiences similar to or different from their own; engage with texts by First Nations Australian authors alongside Australian and world authors and illustrators; identify some cultural features in characters and events.
wider: Compare experiences depicted across two or more stories from different cultural contexts, articulating specific similarities and differences
Engage with First Nations Australian storytelling from multiple sources (print, visual, digital, multimodal) and discuss how stories are told differently across forms
Identify how cultural details in stories (dress, food, daily routines) reveal information about characters' worlds — across texts from different countries or communities
elaborations: engaging with texts that reflect the social and cultural groups to which students belong
comparing experiences depicted in stories by wide-ranging world authors with own experiences
viewing stories by First Nations Australian storytellers from print, visual, digital and multimodal sources
engaging with texts that portray Australian family life in different settings across Australia; for example, suburban and remote settings
identifying some features of culture that are revealed by characters and events in stories; for example, dress, food and daily routines

AC9EFLE02.minimum_width: Share a feeling or thought about one story — orally or through drawing.
AC9EFLE02.typical_width: Respond to stories and share feelings and thoughts about events and characters in multiple ways — drawing, beginning forms of writing, oral discussion; connect events and characters to personal experiences.
wider: Respond to the same story through multiple modes — oral, drawing, movement or drama — and compare what each mode allows
Respond to stories from First Nations Australian authors and compare responses with responses to stories from other cultural contexts
Create a shared class response text (collaborative drawing, dictated writing or digital slideshow) responding to a favourite story
elaborations: using drawing and beginning forms of writing to express personal responses to stories, poems or films
discussing events and characters in texts, and connecting them to their own experiences

AC9EFLE03.minimum_width: Identify at least one type of literary text and name one feature (e.g. a beginning or a character).
AC9EFLE03.typical_width: Recognise different types of literary texts (fairytales, poems, stories); identify features including events, characters, beginnings and endings; recognise typical story openings; explore First Nations Australian cultural patterns of storytelling.
wider: Compare features across different literary text types — what is the same and different between a fairytale, a realistic story and a poem?
Explore First Nations Australian literature from multiple authors and identify distinctive storytelling patterns
Investigate how poetry tells stories and compare this to prose narrative — examining what each form can and cannot do
elaborations: recognising that stories often have similar beginnings; for example, "Once upon a time", "A long, long time ago" in fairytales or introducing the character: "A girl called Amira …"
exploring literature by First Nations Australian authors and their cultural patterns of storytelling
identifying how stories are told in poetry
identifying typical features of fairytales such as princes and princesses or the moral of the story

AC9EFLE04.minimum_width: Explore and attempt to replicate one rhyme, chant or song, attending to its rhythm or sound pattern.
AC9EFLE04.typical_width: Explore and replicate rhythms and sound patterns in poems, rhymes and songs; use music and actions to enhance appreciation; recite rhymes with actions; explore rhythms in First Nations Australian poetry.
wider: Compare rhythmic patterns across different poem types — nursery rhymes, songs, chants — and discuss what is similar and different
Explore rhythms used in First Nations Australian poetry and songs and compare with other Australian or world poetry
Create original short chants or rhymes using a familiar rhythm as a model
elaborations: using music and actions to enhance appreciation of rhymes, poems, chants and songs
reciting rhymes with actions
exploring rhythms used in poems by First Nations Australians

AC9EFLE05.minimum_width: Retell or re-enact one familiar story through play, drawing or performance.
AC9EFLE05.typical_width: Retell and adapt familiar literary texts through play, performance, images or writing; draw and role-play characters or events; sequence pictures (including using digital tools) to retell a story.
wider: Adapt the same story across multiple modes — drama, drawing, digital sequencing and oral retelling — comparing what changes
Retell a story from a different character's perspective, adapting events accordingly
Adapt a familiar story into a different setting or cultural context, discussing what changes and what stays the same
elaborations: drawing and role-playing characters or events
sequencing pictures, which may involve using digital tools, to retell a story

AC9EFLY01.minimum_width: Identify one familiar text and say what it is used for.
AC9EFLY01.typical_width: Identify familiar texts in home, school and community settings; discuss their purposes; connect text features (images, layout, words) to purpose across a small range of text types.
wider: Identify and sort a wide range of texts from multiple settings (home, school, community, digital) and discuss differences in purpose and audience
Explore how the same information might be communicated through different text types (e.g. a verbal instruction vs a label vs a sign)
Investigate texts from First Nations Australian communities — oral stories, community notices, visual narratives — and discuss their purposes and contexts
elaborations: identifying some features that indicate the purposes of familiar texts; for example, a recipe that includes a list of ingredients and numbered instructions

AC9EFLY02.minimum_width: Listen while one other person speaks in a structured situation; use appropriate volume in at least one context.
AC9EFLY02.typical_width: Interact in informal and structured situations using appropriate listening behaviours; contribute ideas in pairs and small groups; alter volume for different contexts (inside/outside, audience); listen to and follow instructions.
wider: Participate in a range of structured interaction formats — paired discussion, small group, whole class, and more formal presentation audience — applying appropriate listening behaviours in each
Explore how listening conventions differ across contexts and cultures — including First Nations Australian conversational protocols where relevant to the class community
Practise imaginative play-based interaction using language for a range of purposes: negotiating, narrating, instructing
elaborations: exchanging ideas with peers in pairs and small groups, engaging in class discussions, listening to others and contributing ideas
showing understanding of appropriate listening behaviour, such as listening without interrupting, and looking at the speaker, if culturally appropriate
altering volume for inside and outside situations and when speaking to an audience
participating in informal interaction situations; for example, play-based experiences that involve the imaginative use of spoken language
listening to and following instructions

AC9EFLY03.minimum_width: Identify at least one difference between an imaginative and an informative text.
AC9EFLY03.typical_width: Identify some differences between imaginative and informative texts; discuss what is 'real' and what is imagined; compare images in imaginative and informative texts; identify and select texts for information purposes.
wider: Compare three or more text types (imaginative, informative, digital) and build a class chart of distinguishing features
Explore how the same topic (e.g. animals) is presented differently in an imaginative story and an informative text — comparing purpose, language and image use
Investigate First Nations Australian texts that serve both imaginative and informative purposes (e.g. oral cultural accounts) and discuss how these blur the distinction
elaborations: talking about what is "real" and what is imagined in texts
identifying and selecting texts for information purposes and commenting on how the text might help with a task
comparing images in imaginative texts with images in informative texts

AC9EFLY04.minimum_width: Navigate a decodable text correctly (left-to-right, top-to-bottom, one word at a time); attempt unknown words using phonics.
AC9EFLY04.typical_width: Read decodable and authentic texts using developing phonic knowledge; monitor meaning using context and emerging grammatical knowledge; navigate text correctly; attempt unknown words using phonics and high-frequency word knowledge; pause or seek support when meaning breaks down.
wider: Apply reading strategies across a range of decodable and authentic texts at gradually increasing complexity
Read both print and simple digital texts, navigating each appropriately
Read texts with culturally diverse content — including First Nations Australian authored texts — and apply strategies to unfamiliar vocabulary in context
elaborations: navigating a text correctly, starting at the right place and reading in the right direction, returning to the next line as needed and matching one spoken word to one written word
attempting to work out unknown words by using phonic decoding and knowledge of high-frequency words
pausing or asking for support when meaning breaks down

AC9EFLY05.minimum_width: Use at least one comprehension strategy (e.g. predicting or connecting) when listening to or reading a text.
AC9EFLY05.typical_width: Use a range of comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, questioning — when listening, viewing and reading; retell stories and informative texts using picture cues or prompts; relate key facts from informative texts; sequence events from First Nations Australians' stories.
wider: Apply comprehension strategies across different text types — stories, informative texts, poems, visual texts — and compare what strategies are most useful for each
Use strategies with increasing independence across a range of text complexities
Retell and discuss First Nations Australian stories and cultural accounts, attending to cultural sequence and significance
elaborations: sequencing ideas in spoken texts, retelling well-known stories, retelling stories with picture cues, retelling information using prompts
listening for specific purposes; for example, details of a character or to answer a given question
relating one or two key facts from informative texts
retelling events from First Nations Australians' stories and cultural accounts in sequence
predicting what might happen in a text based on the title and cover

AC9EFLY06.minimum_width: Create a short written text (using beginning writing knowledge) that records an idea or event; include at least one capital letter at the start of a sentence.
AC9EFLY06.typical_width: Create and participate in shared editing of short written texts to record and report ideas and events; use some learnt vocabulary, basic sentence boundary punctuation and spell some CVC words correctly; use writing and drawing including digital tools; 'read' own texts back.
wider: Create texts for different purposes — recording an event, reporting an observation, expressing a personal response — applying vocabulary and punctuation knowledge in each
Create multimodal texts using digital tools that combine writing and images, attending to how each mode contributes to meaning
Create texts in response to First Nations Australian stories or cultural accounts, using drawing and writing to convey ideas
elaborations: using beginning writing knowledge, sound–letter relationships, known words and punctuation to create short texts
using writing and drawing, which may include digital tools, to represent and communicate personal responses to ideas and events experienced through texts
"reading" their own texts back to an experienced writer
participating in shared editing by circling the capital letters at the beginning of sentences

AC9EFLY07.minimum_width: Deliver a very short spoken text (2–3 sentences) to peers using an appropriate volume.
AC9EFLY07.typical_width: Create and deliver short spoken texts to report ideas and events to peers; use appropriate volume; share personal experiences, interests or discoveries in semi-formal situations; use visual prompts to stay on topic or sequence ideas.
wider: Deliver spoken texts for different purposes — sharing a personal experience, reporting on a text, expressing a preference — in different contexts
Use a range of visual and physical prompts (objects, drawings, digital images) to support oral delivery
Deliver a spoken response to a First Nations Australian story or cultural account, attending to culturally appropriate ways of sharing
elaborations: sharing a personal experience, interest or discovery with peers in a semi-formal situation
sharing personal responses to ideas and events experienced through texts
using visual prompts to practise staying on topic or to sequence ideas

AC9EFLY08.minimum_width: Form most lower-case letters using learnt formations, with reasonable legibility.
AC9EFLY08.typical_width: Form most lower-case and upper-case letters using learnt letter formations; demonstrate functional pencil grip.
wider: Practise letter formation across multiple media — pencil, whiteboard marker, sand tray, digital stylus — attending to consistency of formation
Apply learnt letter formations in the context of real writing tasks (labelling drawings, writing names, copying short sentences)
Explore how letter formation connects to print conventions — size, spacing, directionality — in different text contexts
AC9EFLY08.width_notes: Thin width for formation accuracy itself — the skill does not broaden across contexts at Foundation. Wider directions focus on application contexts and modalities rather than formal enrichment.
elaborations: following clear demonstrations of how to construct each letter; for example, where to start and in which direction to write
developing a functional pencil grip/grasp

AC9EFLY09.minimum_width: Recognise and produce a rhyming pair; clap syllables in a two-syllable word; isolate a phoneme in a spoken word.
AC9EFLY09.typical_width: Recognise and generate rhyming words; identify alliteration patterns; identify syllables in spoken words; isolate and identify individual phonemes (sounds) in spoken words.
wider: Generate rhyming strings across multiple word families — exploring how the same rime pattern appears across many words
Investigate alliteration across poem types and student-created word lists
Explore phonological patterns in words from other languages or First Nations Australian languages, attending to similarities and differences with English patterns
elaborations: recognising and producing rhyming words when listening to rhyming stories or rhymes; for example, "funny" and "money"
identifying patterns of alliteration in spoken words; for example, "helpful Henry"
identifying syllables in spoken words; for example, clapping the rhythm of "Mon-day", "Ja-cob" or "Si-en-na"

AC9EFLY10.minimum_width: Segment a single-syllable word into its phonemes (say the sounds); blend a sequence of phonemes into a word.
AC9EFLY10.typical_width: Segment sentences into individual words; blend and segment single-syllable spoken words; isolate, blend and manipulate phonemes — including addition, deletion and substitution at initial, medial and final positions.
wider: Apply blending and segmenting to a wide range of single-syllable word types — CVC, CVCC, CCVC — building a broad phoneme manipulation repertoire
Practise phoneme manipulation through word games, chants and minimal pairs — expanding the range of phonemes encountered
Explore phoneme patterns in words from culturally diverse contexts — names, place names, First Nations Australian words — applying blending and segmenting strategies
elaborations: saying the sounds when given a word; for example, "can" ("c-a-n") or "ship" ("sh-i-p")
saying the word when given the sounds; for example, "l-i-p" ("lip") or "m-u-n-ch" ("munch")
saying the new word when the beginning phoneme/medial/end phoneme in a word is replaced with a different phoneme; for example, "run" becomes "fun", or "fun" becomes "fan"

AC9EFLY11.minimum_width: Name and recognise most upper- and lower-case letters; identify the most common sound for at least half of the letters.
AC9EFLY11.typical_width: Recognise and name all upper- and lower-case letters; know the most common sound each letter represents; match upper- and lower-case letter pairs.
wider: Identify letters and their sounds across a range of fonts and handwriting styles — recognising that the same letter takes different visual forms
Recognise own name letters in different contexts and connect letter identity to letter-sound knowledge
Explore letters and their sounds in contexts beyond English — for example, recognising that other writing systems have different letter-sound conventions
AC9EFLY11.width_notes: Thin width — this is a knowledge acquisition standard with limited contextual breadth. Wider directions focus on application contexts and variation in visual form rather than enrichment in the traditional sense.
elaborations: recognising letters in own name
matching upper- and lower-case letters
identifying sounds for upper- and lower-case letters

AC9EFLY12.minimum_width: Write and read at least five CVC words accurately.
AC9EFLY12.typical_width: Write CVC words by representing sounds with appropriate letters; blend sounds associated with letters when reading CVC words across a range of short vowel patterns.
wider: Write and read CVC words across all short vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u) — building a broad initial decoding repertoire
Apply CVC knowledge in the context of real reading and writing tasks — labelling, writing captions, reading decodable texts
Compare CVC word families and identify shared rimes — connecting phonics knowledge to word recognition
AC9EFLY12.width_notes: No elaborations provided for this descriptor. Wider directions inferred from typical CVC instructional scope at Foundation level.

AC9EFLY13.minimum_width: Attempt to spell an unknown word using letter-sound correspondences, producing a plausible attempt.
AC9EFLY13.typical_width: Use knowledge of letters and sounds to spell words; make plausible spelling choices using letter-sound correspondences; apply morphemic knowledge where relevant.
wider: Apply letter-sound spelling strategies across a range of word types encountered in different writing contexts — labelling, sentence writing, text creation
Investigate word spelling across multiple topics, applying letter-sound strategies to new vocabulary
Explore spelling patterns in words from different languages — for example, names from diverse cultural backgrounds — and discuss where English letter-sound rules apply and where they don't
elaborations: making plausible spelling choices using letter–sound correspondences and morphemic knowledge

AC9EFLY14.minimum_width: Read and write at least five high-frequency words.
AC9EFLY14.typical_width: Read and write an increasing number of high-frequency words encountered in shared and independent reading texts; recognise some familiar words (own name, character names, school name).
wider: Build and read a personal word bank of high-frequency words encountered across multiple texts and topics
Apply high-frequency word knowledge in independent writing and check own spelling in context
Investigate how high-frequency words appear across different text types — books, signs, labels, digital texts — building multi-context recognition
elaborations: knowing how to read and write some high-frequency words recognised in shared texts and texts being read independently; for example, "and", "my", "is", "the" and "go"
knowing how to read and write some familiar words; for example, their name, the name of a character or the name of their school

AC9EFLY15.minimum_width: Recognise that a word is a unit of meaning; identify one example of a word made of more than one meaningful part.
AC9EFLY15.typical_width: Understand that words are units of meaning; recognise that words can be made of more than one meaningful part (e.g. 'dogs' = 'dog' + 's').
wider: Identify two-part words across a range of word types — plurals, simple verb endings — building awareness of morphemic structure
Explore compound words (e.g. 'sunflower', 'raincoat') as another form of multi-part words
Investigate words with meaningful parts from other languages familiar to students — discussing how different languages build meaning through word parts
elaborations: learning that words are made up of meaningful parts; for example, "dogs" has 2 meaningful parts: "dog" and "s" meaning more than one
